newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia forces exchange fire, PM rules out war.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia forces exchange fire, PM rules out war.

text.p: Gunshots and explosions echoed across Phnom Penh on Saturday as rival government troops clashed northwest of the city but Second Prime Minister Hun Sen said the fighting did not signal civil war.
The blasts could be heard in the centre of the capital, some five km (three miles) from the fighting.
The shooting subsided in the afternoon and broke out again before dusk. The explosions were reported near the home of a top general loyal to First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
"We can hear loud explosions. I think they are B-40 rockets coming from the area of Nhiek Bun Chhay's house," said a reporter.
The general is Ranariddh's top military adviser.
Witnesses also said troops loyal to Hun Sen appeared to be moving towards a military base controlled by Ranariddh's forces near the airport, about six km (four miles) from the general's home.
The soldiers exchanged shots near the base about 12 km (eight miles) northwest of the capital, a military official loyal to Ranariddh said earlier.

"The fighting is starting now. CPP troops have come to our base," said the military official inside the base, referring to troops loyal to Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP), the former communist government.
There were no immediate reports of casualties.
The upsurge of violence prompted the closure of Phnom Penh airport, a Thai Airways ticket agent said in Bangkok. But sources at the airport could not confirm the closure.
Cambodia's chief of general staff ordered forces loyal to Hun Sen to take control of roads and clear what he described as "illegal checkpoints".

"All armed forces units, military police have to cooperate with national police and local authorities to take measures to increase contol at checkpoints to prevent the movement of illegal weapons and forces into towns and the capital," General Keo Kimyan said in a radio broadcast.
Hun Sen on Saturday repeated his accusation that Ranariddh was trying to smuggle defectors from the dreaded Khmer Rouge guerrilla movement into Phnom Penh.
"I do not allow anyone in any position to destroy the country's future," Hun Sen said in a radio broadcast.
Both prime ministers were out of the country on Saturday, their offices said, and it was not immediately clear from where Hun Sen made his radio broadcast.
The Vietnamese Foreign Ministry said on Saturday Hun Sen was on holiday in Vietnam.

"I would like to declare publicly that this is the activity of law implementation by the armed forces of the government against law violators and illegal forces and this is not a civil war," Hun Sen said.
Officials in Ranariddh's office denied that the prince's military commanders were bringing Khmer Rouge defectors into Phnom Penh.
"They are the ones creating disorder," Ly Thuch, the head of Ranariddh's cabinet, told Reuters. "They want to destroy our democracy. Our democracy is in danger."

Ranariddh and Hun Sen, former battlefield foes when Hun Sen was with the Khmer Rouge, joined in a ruling coalition after U.N.-sponsored polls in 1993. The next general election is scheduled for May 1998.

But the relationship has become increasingly fractious. Analysts say the two are jockeying for position ahead of the May polls when the allegiance of defectors of the disintegrating Khmer Rouge is expected to be a major factor.

The Khmer Rouge ruled from 1975-1979 in what has popularly become know as the "killing fields" reign of terror under which more than a million Cambodians died through torture, execution, starvation or disease.
